entries.text:
You speak plainly, without a flourish, and for once without a single embroidered word. When you're done, the hall is so quiet the gulls on the quay are loud.

Rehearsing gave you advantage, and the exhaustion that has dogged you since the road gave you disadvantage. They cancel, so it's a plain roll. Your Persuasion check was an 18, and it carries.

The arbiter lets the silence sit. Then she turns the Dray leaf over, reads the Thistlewood letter again, and lays Elowen's commission-paper down last, not reading it, only looking at the lantern in the wax. "You kept a thief's book two weeks," she says. "You might have sold it, or ransomed it, or burned it. You came to this hall and set it in my hand with your name." She takes up her stylus. "The hall of Vantry lays no charge on you. The leaves and the clerk's case go under my seal to Dame Crowe's assize, and Sir Corwen's reeve will read the contract against the keep's rolls." She looks at the Vantry elder. "And the sealing stays unset until the two young people say, of their own mouths, what they want."

Isaude stands up before her father can speak. "Of my own mouth," she says, and the elder's son, red to the ears, says, "And mine," and it seems that for the first time that day nobody in the hall is lying. Sir Corwen sits down heavily and puts his face in his hand.

Then the arbiter points her stylus at the cellar door. "A quarter hour," she says, "with a guard on the stair. Not a minute over."

It is twenty to three. The guard unlocks the heavy cellar door and lights a lantern. Kit comes with you down the stone steps, which smell of tar, salt and cold stone. At the foot is a low vaulted room with barrels along the walls, and in the middle of it, on an upturned cask, Corvin Tallowmere sits with his gloved hands in his lap, as comfortable as a man at his own fireside. His wrists are bound before him with a cord, not iron. The guard stops halfway down the stair and folds his arms.

Corvin looks up and smiles his gentle smile again. "You read it, didn't you?" he says. "The paper. I can see it in your face." He tilts his head. "Sit down, my dear. You asked for a quarter hour. Ask me what you came to ask."

What does Wren say?

Arbiter keeps the Dray leaf and clerk's case as evidence, orders Wren to remain in Saltmarsh until the Marrowford assize or a writ from Dame Crowe, and gives her the promised quarter hour with Corvin in the cellar (guard at the door, Kit may stand by). Arbiter read Elowen's commission-paper and said the Wick-House keeper should be asked to attest it.

entries.text:
You begin plainly, as you promised yourself, and for a while it goes well. The hall is quiet while you name the houses, Verrel, Thistlewood and Dray, and the Vantry elder shifts uneasily at the third.

But the words won't hold their order. Your Persuasion check was a 7. The rehearsal's help and the weight of exhaustion cancel each other out, and the roll itself was poor. You lose your place between the Thistlewood ford and the Thornhallow register, and have to start the sentence again. When you slide the commission-paper forward, you do it a beat too eagerly, and a murmur runs along the benches. A girl showing a dead priest's will in a merchant's hall looks to some like a girl with a story to sell.

The arbiter lets you finish. She reads the commission-paper twice, then sets it down by the Dray leaf without comment. She is not unkind, but she is precise.

"What I have heard is a confession of theft and a request for faith," she says. "The page is sound. The prisoner has admitted it before the hall. That much stands." She taps the ledger leaf. "This hall keeps the Dray leaf as evidence, and the clerk's case. You will not leave Saltmarsh until Dame Crowe's assize at Marrowford or a writ in her hand releases you, and you will say so in front of the Lantern-Bearer's shrine, since you claim one." She slides the commission-paper back across the table. "The keeper of the Wick-House should be asked to attest this. I'll not stand between a priest's heir and her staff, if she is one."

Sir Corwen says nothing as you sit, but Isaude reaches across the aisle and touches your sleeve for a heartbeat.

"Quarter of an hour," the arbiter adds, "as promised. The cellar. One guard at the door. Your companion may stand beside you."

It's twenty to three. The cellar guard is already holding the heavy door open, and a stair goes down into lamplight and the smell of cold stone and tar. Somewhere at the bottom, a calm voice is humming the road song you taught Kit. The Wick-House is just down the quay.

What does Wren do?

entries.text:
You stand, set the psalter on the table and tell it plainly. You tell the hall about nineteen years of tales, the ledger, the three houses, and the two weeks you kept it. You don't perform. You lay out Verrel and Thistlewood in order, the page burned and the ford confessed, and then slide the Dray leaf and Elowen's paper into the light.

Your Persuasion check was a 10. Your rehearsal and your exhaustion cancelled out, so it was a straight roll, and it isn't enough to carry the room.

The arbiter listens to all of it without moving. Then she says, "It is a good account. It is also the account a clever girl would give." She lifts a hand before Sir Corwen can speak. "I believe the page. I cannot yet believe the bearer. So: I keep the Dray leaf and the clerk's case in the hall's seal. My clerk will copy your Thistlewood leaf and Osric's entry, and you will keep your originals. You will remain in Saltmarsh until Dame Crowe's assize or the keep's justice calls for you, and you'll lodge twenty gold pieces with the hall as a bond, returned if you're found honest."

Sir Corwen rises heavily. "I'll stand surety for the girl," he says, "if she'll lodge with my steward. My daughter says her word's good enough for the ledger. It is good enough for me to be ashamed in front of." Isaude gives you a brief, almost shy smile.

The arbiter allows it with a thin nod. "The sealing is stayed. Sir Corwen's reeve will read the contract against the keep's rolls tomorrow. Mistress Ashgrove." She looks at you a long moment. "You have your quarter hour with the prisoner, as I promised. The guard will stand at the door."

It is twenty-three minutes to three. The cellar door at the back of the hall is open, and the guard waits beside it, one hand on his keys. Down the quay, you know, stands the Wick-House with your mother's lamp-staff in its keeping. Kit is at your shoulder, and you still have 54 gold pieces and four silver after the bond, if you pay it.

What does Wren do?

You sleep the afternoon away by the fire, boots off, with Kit snoring across the room. The storm blows itself thin against the shutters. This isn't a long rest. Your slots stay empty, your Bardic Inspiration at one, and the weight of exhaustion is still on you when you wake. It is nearly six when Pell knocks.

He hands you a folded sheet, still faintly damp, and goes to stand by the door with his halberd, looking at nothing. Kit sits up, rubs her face, and says, "Supper first." Bess sets bread, fish pie and a jug of small beer on the table, and you read by the lamp while Kit eats.

She kept a book. Ask for the wren-page. I paid her for you. Whatever you think of me, the first part of that was true.*

What does Wren do?

Kit wakes, sits up and looks at the map. "Two days up the road," she says. "Or we could wait for the rider's answer about Aldous."

You sleep through the afternoon beside the fire with your boots steaming on the hearth and Kit snoring across the room. It's a rest of sorts, though not the long rest that restores your magic. It's nearly seven when Pell knocks, wet to the knees, with the rain thinning behind him. He hands over a folded sheet without a word and goes back down to the taproom for his own supper.

Corvin's hand is steady, and the paper is clean. It's a rough map of the lower Marrow, with a note under it:

*Reedmouth Ferry, a day's ride upriver of Saltmarsh, on the west bank. The Lamp-House stands at the landing, a small shrine with a brass lantern over the door. I left the child there with Goodwife Anneth Cray, who kept her two winters on Elowen's coin. Anneth took her pay and left for the coast years ago, so ask the ferryman, not the shrine. I do not know where she went. I took you in the spring of the second winter, and I paid her eleven silver. Write what you will of me. C.T.*

You read it by the lamp and set it beside Elowen's letter and the strip from the lamp-staff. Elowen's letter says her daughter was left "safe among people who will love her, far from the man who sells lanterns." That fits a shrine-house, and a road-priest would choose one of her own faith. The brass lantern drawn over the Lamp-House door is the crooked-flame kind that Marta Pell has at Lantern's Rest, the "same hand" Corvin once spoke of. Nothing in it contradicts what you hold. It also can't be checked from here, and Corvin's best tales always had a clean, plausible spine.

Kit wakes, eats stew without comment, and listens. Over supper the real choices lie open:

Reedmouth is a day upriver, on the road back toward Marrowford, and it holds the oldest trail to your own beginning. Brann's lamp is the other pull. The reliquary is still in its socket on the spit, and the squall should clear by morning, so Dunn could take you across. Then there's the long wait for Lord Edric's answer about "Aldous," and Dame Crowe's assize at month's end, with Corvin to bring to Marrowford alive. Whatever you choose, your long rest can't finish before about four tomorrow morning, and you still have no spell slots.

input.description: Small roadside shrine-house of the Lantern-Bearer at the Withy Ferry crossing on the lower Marrow, about a day upriver of Saltmarsh. Per Corvin's map (Day 10 dusk, unverified): Elowen left the child Wren here with Goody Annet Marsh, who kept foundlings for coin. Corvin paid her more and took the child. His postscript says a lean man asked after the child there some years later.
relationships: named on [[Corvin Tallowmere]]'s hand-drawn map as where Wren was left as a small child

You go back up to the Salt Gull, peel off your wet boots and sleep the afternoon away by the fire, with Kit snoring across the room. It is a good sleep, but it's an afternoon's nap and not a long rest. Your slots stay empty, and the weariness sits where it was.

Pell comes at dusk, as he promised, with rain on his helm and a folded sheet inside his tabard. "Straight from his hand to mine," he says. "I watched him write it." Then he goes, awkward and stiff, before you can thank him.

You read it by the lamp. It's a map drawn with a steady hand, and it's plain. A river bend is marked *Withy Ferry*, and beside the ferry stands a small house with a little crooked flame drawn over the door. Under it Corvin has written:

*Rushlight House. One long day's ride upriver of Saltmarsh, on the left bank. Goody Annet Marsh kept foundlings for coin and asked nothing. Elowen left you there with a silver penny and the words "until I send." Nobody sent. I came instead. I paid her twice what Elowen did.*

And below, smaller: *Some years after, a lean man asked at that door for a girl with Elowen's chin. Annet told him nothing. I do not know if she is living. C.*

You lay it beside Elowen's letter and the strip from the staff. Neither names the place. Elowen's letter says only that you were "safe among people who will love her", and a house that took coin for foundlings isn't quite what that sounds like. It could be a lie, or it could be what she believed or had to settle for. The crooked flame over the door is right, at least. It's the Lantern-Bearer's mark, and it's also Elowen's. A lean man asking is Sparrow-shaped, but you can't be sure.

Kit sits across from you with a bowl of Bess's fish stew. She reads the map upside down and says, "Day's ride. Horses are at the livery." She chews. "Man in the grey cloak knows we're here. Might know about that house too."

Over supper the choices are laid out. You could ride at first light for Withy Ferry, which is also upriver toward Marrowford and the assize. You could go back to the spit for the reliquary once the storm clears and the sea is calm. Or you could stay a day for your long rest and the arbiter's rider to return. Either way you finish your long rest properly tomorrow before dawn, at about four.

It is six in the evening, and the rain has eased. What does Wren do?
